q: A ketone C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>16</sub>O gives the mass spectrum shown: M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 128, base peak at m/z 57, and strong peaks at m/z 99 and 72. Which ketone is it?
h: α-Cleavage on each side of the C=O gives two acylium ions. A McLafferty rearrangement gives an even-mass ion. Predict all three for each choice.
w: For a ketone R–CO–R′, α-cleavage gives R–C≡O+ and R′–C≡O+, and a γ-hydrogen gives a McLafferty ion at even m/z. 3-Octanone (ethyl pentyl ketone): losing the pentyl radical (71) gives CH3CH2C≡O+ at m/z 57; losing the ethyl radical (29) gives C5H11C≡O+ at m/z 99; and the γ-H on the pentyl side lets 1-butene (56) leave, giving the enol radical cation at m/z 72. All three match: 3-octanone.
x: 4-Octanone gives acylium ions at m/z 71 (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>7</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) and 85 (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>9</sub>CO<sup>+</sup>) and McLafferty ions at 86 and 100, not 57, 99 and 72.
2-Octanone (a methyl ketone) gives CH<sub>3</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at m/z 43 as the base peak, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>13</sub>CO<sup>+</sup> at 113, and a McLafferty ion at 58.
This ketone gives a strong m/z 57 (the tert-butyl cation), but its acylium ions are at 85 and 71 and its McLafferty ion is at 100; it cannot give 99 or 72.

q: How many signals appear in the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of 4′-isopropylacetophenone (shown)?
h: Use the mirror plane through C1 and C4 of the ring. How many kinds of ring H, and are the two isopropyl methyls equivalent?
w: The molecule has a mirror plane through the two ring carbons that carry substituents. Signals: the acetyl CH3 (singlet, 3H); two kinds of aromatic H (2H each, the pair next to C=O and the pair next to the isopropyl); the isopropyl CH (septet, 1H); and the two isopropyl CH3 groups, which are equivalent (doublet, 6H). Total: 5.
x: Four misses one set: the ring H next to the acetyl group and those next to the isopropyl group are in different environments.
Six counts the two isopropyl methyls separately; they are swapped by the mirror plane and give one 6H doublet.
Seven treats all four ring H as different; the mirror plane makes them two pairs.

q: Which C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>O ether gives exactly three signals in its broadband-decoupled <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum?
h: Look for symmetry that makes the two sides of the oxygen the same, then count carbons on one side.
w: Dipropyl ether is symmetric about the oxygen, so the two propyl groups are equivalent and each gives three kinds of carbon: OCH2, CH2, CH3. Dipropyl ether shows three 13C signals.
x: Diisopropyl ether is also symmetric, but each isopropyl has only two kinds of carbon (CH and the two equivalent CH<sub>3</sub>), so it gives two signals.
tert-Butyl ethyl ether has four kinds of carbon: OCH2, CH3 of ethyl, the quaternary C and the three equivalent CH3.
1-Methoxypentane has no symmetry; all six carbons are different.

q: The 13C NMR spectrum of 4-methoxy-2-butanone (shown) has peaks at δ 207.0, 67.9, 58.8, 43.6 and 30.4. Which set gives the shifts of the tagged carbons a, b, c and d, in that order?
h: Ketone C=O near 200+; sp<sup>3</sup> carbons bonded to O at 50–70; sp<sup>3</sup> carbons next to C=O at 30–45.
w: The ketone carbon b is the peak at 207.0. The two carbons bonded to O are 67.9 (the OCH2, untagged) and 58.8 (the OCH3, d). Of the carbons next to the C=O, the CH2 c (43.6) is farther downfield than the CH3 a (30.4), because it has an extra carbon attached and is also β to oxygen. a 30.4, b 207.0, c 43.6, d 58.8.
x: This swaps c and d: the OCH<sub>3</sub> is bonded directly to oxygen and belongs in the 50–70 region, while the CH<sub>2</sub> next to the C=O is near 44.
A methyl next to a C=O is not bonded to oxygen, so it is not at 58.8; that shift belongs to the OCH<sub>3</sub> (d).
Carbon d is the methoxy CH<sub>3</sub> (58.8); 67.9 is the OCH<sub>2</sub>, which is not tagged. And the CH<sub>3</sub> (a) is the most upfield carbon, 30.4.

q: Which compounds give a <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum consisting of only one triplet and one quartet (no other signals)?
h: A triplet plus a quartet is one ethyl group. Only one signal pair means every ethyl group must be equivalent.
w: A CH3CH2– group gives a 3H triplet and a 2H quartet. I (3-pentanone) has two ethyl groups made equivalent by symmetry: one triplet, one quartet. II (ethyl propanoate) has two different ethyl groups, the acyl CH2 near 2.3 and the OCH2 near 4.1, so it shows two triplets and two quartets. III (diethyl carbonate) is symmetric: one OCH2 quartet and one CH3 triplet. I and III only.
x: III also qualifies: the two ethoxy groups of diethyl carbonate are equivalent, giving one triplet and one quartet.
II does not qualify: its two ethyl groups are on different sides of the ester and give four signals.
I qualifies (its two ethyls are equivalent), and II does not (four signals).

q: Rank the 1H NMR signals of the hydrogens on the tagged carbons of 3-chloropropanal from lowest to highest chemical shift.
h: Recall the typical ranges: H next to C=O about 2–3 ppm, H on a carbon bearing Cl about 3.5–4, aldehyde H about 9.5–10.
w: The aldehyde H on a is strongly deshielded by the C=O anisotropy and electronegativity (δ ≈ 9.8). The CH2 bonded to Cl, c, appears near 3.8. The CH2 next to the carbonyl, b, appears near 2.9. Lowest to highest: b < c < a.
x: Cl is bonded directly to c, which deshields it more than the C=O deshields the α-CH<sub>2</sub> b, so c lies downfield of b.
This is the reverse order; the aldehyde H is the most downfield signal, not the most upfield.
The aldehyde H (about 9.8) lies far downfield of the CH<sub>2</sub>Cl (about 3.8).

q: A compound C<sub>9</sub>H<sub>11</sub>NO<sub>2</sub> gives the <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum shown (the 2H signal at δ 4.05 is broad and disappears when D<sub>2</sub>O is added). Which structure is it?
h: Two 2H doublets in the aromatic region point to one substitution pattern. Then decide where the ethyl group is attached from the shift of its quartet.
w: Two aromatic doublets of 2H each mean a para-disubstituted ring. The 2H quartet at 4.32 with a 3H triplet at 1.36 is an ethyl group on an ester oxygen (OCH2, deshielded by O and C=O). The exchangeable 2H broad singlet is an NH2. The doublet at 6.64 is ortho to the electron-donating NH2 (shielded) and the one at 7.86 is ortho to the ester C=O. This is ethyl 4-aminobenzoate (benzocaine).
x: An ortho-disubstituted ring has four different aromatic H (1H each), not two 2H doublets.
An N-ethyl group's CH<sub>2</sub> appears near 3.2, not 4.3; the acid would also show a COOH near 12 ppm and the NH would be 1H, not 2H.
This compound has two methyl singlets (OCH<sub>3</sub> and NCH<sub>3</sub>) and no ethyl quartet or triplet.

q: A compound C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O gives the <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shown; the DEPT result (C, CH, CH<sub>2</sub> or CH<sub>3</sub>) is written over each peak. Which structure is it?
h: There is no CH<sub>3</sub> peak, and there are two CH<sub>2</sub> peaks. Which choice has no methyl group?
w: Four aromatic peaks (one C and three CH) mean a monosubstituted benzene ring. The sp3 region has two CH2 carbons and no CH3: one at 63.7 (bonded to O) and one at 39.2 (benzylic, not bonded to O). That is Ph–CH2–CH2–OH, 2-phenylethanol.
x: 1-Phenylethanol would show a CH (bonded to O, near 70) and a CH<sub>3</sub> (near 25), not two CH<sub>2</sub> peaks.
Benzyl methyl ether would show a CH<sub>3</sub> (OCH<sub>3</sub> near 58) and only one CH<sub>2</sub> (near 75).
4-Ethylphenol has a CH<sub>3</sub> and a para-disubstituted ring (two aromatic C peaks, one near 153 for C–OH, and only two CH peaks).

q: An alcohol C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O shows a broad IR band at 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>. With chromic acid (Jones reagent) the orange solution turns green, and the isolated product shows a strong IR band at 1715 cm<sup>−1</sup> and no O–H band. Which alcohol was it?
h: Which kinds of alcohol does chromic acid oxidize, and what does each give? Does the product still have an O–H?
w: Chromic acid (Cr(VI), orange) is reduced to Cr(III) (green) when it oxidizes an alcohol that has an H on the carbinol carbon. A secondary alcohol gives a ketone (C=O near 1715, no O–H), while a primary alcohol is oxidized all the way to a carboxylic acid (C=O plus a very broad O–H at 2500–3300). The product here is a ketone, 2-butanone, so the alcohol was 2-butanol.
x: tert-Butyl alcohol has no H on the carbinol carbon, so it does not react with chromic acid (the solution stays orange).
1-Butanol is oxidized by aqueous chromic acid to butanoic acid, which still shows a very broad O–H band.
Diethyl ether has no O–H band to begin with and is not oxidized by chromic acid.

q: Which compound gives the IR spectrum shown? (There is no absorption above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>.)
h: Identify the band near 2250 and the band near 1715. Then rule out any choice that would add a band the spectrum lacks.
w: The sharp medium band at 2250 cm−1 is a C≡N stretch, and the strong band at 1715 cm−1 is a ketone C=O. Nothing appears above 3000 cm−1, so there is no O–H and no ≡C–H. 5-Oxohexanenitrile (a ketone and a nitrile) fits.
x: A terminal alkyne shows a strong, sharp ≡C–H stretch near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a weak C≡C near 2120, not a band at 2250 with nothing above 3000.
An alcohol would give a broad O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and this compound has no C=O for the 1715 band.
An ester C=O appears near 1740 cm<sup>−1</sup>, with a strong C–O band near 1240; the spectrum's C=O is at 1715.

q: A compound gives the mass spectrum and IR spectrum shown. MS: m/z 154 and 156 (3 : 1), base peak 139 with a partner at 141 (3 : 1), and 111/113 (3 : 1). IR: strong band at 1685 cm<sup>−1</sup>, weak band at 3060 cm<sup>−1</sup>, nothing near 3300 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Which structure fits?
h: Each 3 : 1 pair contains one Cl. Which fragment keeps the Cl, and what was lost to make the base peak?
w: The 3 : 1 pairs show one chlorine, and the molecular ion is at 154. The 1685 cm−1 band is a conjugated (aryl) ketone C=O, and 3060 is aromatic C–H. The base peak at 139/141 is M − 15: loss of CH3• by α-cleavage, giving ClC6H4–C≡O+, which still has Cl. Losing CO from it gives ClC6H4+ at 111/113. This is 4′-chloroacetophenone.
x: 2-Chloroacetophenone also has M = 154/156, but α-cleavage loses •CH<sub>2</sub>Cl and gives PhC≡O<sup>+</sup> at m/z 105 with no chlorine partner; the base peak would not be a 139/141 pair.
4-Chlorobenzaldehyde has M = 140/142, not 154/156.
1-(4-Chlorophenyl)ethanol has M = 156/158 and an O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and it has no C=O to absorb at 1685.

q: A compound C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>O gives these data. Which structure fits?
h: The sharp 3290 band and the 1H triplet go together. A small (2–3 Hz) coupling can pass through a C≡C.
w: The strong, sharp 3290 cm−1 band with a weak 2120 band is a terminal alkyne (≡C–H and C≡C). No broad O–H band and a strong 1100 C–O band mean an ether. In the 1H NMR, the 3H singlet at 3.39 is OCH3; the 2H doublet at 4.13 is an O–CH2 next to the alkyne; the 1H triplet at 2.43 is the ≡C–H. The CH2 and ≡C–H split each other through the triple bond (long-range coupling, J ≈ 2.4 Hz). 3-Methoxyprop-1-yne (methyl propargyl ether).
x: 2-Butyn-1-ol has an O–H (broad band near 3350) and no ≡C–H; its CH<sub>3</sub> would be near 1.8, not an OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet at 3.39.
3-Butyn-1-ol has an O–H band and two CH<sub>2</sub> groups, with no OCH<sub>3</sub> singlet.
1-Methoxyprop-1-yne is an internal alkyne with no ≡C–H, so it would have no 3290 band and no 1H signal; it gives two 3H singlets.

q: A compound that contains only C, H and O shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 88. Combustion analysis gives 54.5% carbon by mass. What is its molecular formula?
h: Multiply the molar mass by the mass fraction of carbon to find the mass of carbon in one mole, then divide by 12.
w: Mass of C per mole = 0.545 × 88 = 48 g, which is 48/12 = 4 carbons. The remaining 40 mass units must be H and O: 2 O (32) + 8 H (8) = 40. The formula is C4H8O2 (DBE 1, for example an ester or a carboxylic acid). Check: 48.04/88.11 = 54.5% C.
x: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O also has M = 88, but it is 60/88 = 68.1% carbon.
C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>O<sub>3</sub> also has M = 88, but it is 36/88 = 40.9% carbon.
C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>4</sub> has M = 88 but is 95.4% carbon and contains no oxygen; it is also an unlikely highly unsaturated formula.

q: Hexanal (M = 100) shows a prominent peak at m/z 44 in its mass spectrum, formed by a McLafferty rearrangement. Which ion is it, and what neutral molecule is lost?
h: The C=O oxygen takes the H on the γ-carbon (tag d), and the bond between the α- and β-carbons (b–c) breaks.
w: In a McLafferty rearrangement, the carbonyl O removes a γ-hydrogen (on carbon d) through a six-membered transition state, and the bond between the α-carbon (b) and β-carbon (c) breaks. The β- and γ-carbons and the rest of the chain leave as an alkene, CH2=CH–CH2CH3 (1-butene, 56), and the ion kept is the enol radical cation of acetaldehyde: CH2=CH–OH•+, m/z 44, with loss of 1-butene. 100 − 56 = 44.
x: The H moves to oxygen, so the ion is first formed as the enol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–OH<sup>•+</sup>, not as the keto form.
The neutral fragment is an alkene (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, 56), not an alkane; 100 − 58 would give m/z 42, not 44.
This ion has lost an H from the wrong place and has m/z 42; the McLafferty ion keeps all the H it started with plus the transferred H.

q: Which compound shows two N–H stretching bands of medium intensity near 3300 and 3380 cm<sup>−1</sup>?
h: Count the H atoms on nitrogen. Two N–H bonds can stretch in phase and out of phase.
w: A primary amine, R–NH2, has two N–H bonds that stretch together in a symmetric and an asymmetric mode, giving two bands near 3300 and 3380 cm−1. Cyclohexylamine is the primary amine.
x: A secondary amine has only one N–H, so it shows a single weak band.
A tertiary amine has no N–H bond and no band in this region.
An alcohol gives one broad, strong O–H band near 3350 cm<sup>−1</sup>, not two medium N–H bands.

q: A compound C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O<sub>2</sub> shows strong IR bands at 1720 and 1160 cm<sup>−1</sup> and a medium band at 1638 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum is shown (the two vinyl singlets are each 1H, from two different =CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens). Which structure is it?
h: DBE 2: one C=O and one C=C. All four signals are singlets, so no hydrogen-bearing carbons are neighbors.
w: DBE = 2. The 1720 band is a C=O, 1638 a C=C, and 1160 a C–O, so this is an unsaturated ester. Every signal is a singlet: OCH3 (3.75), a CH3 on an alkene carbon (1.95), and two separate vinyl H (6.10 and 5.56) that are on the same carbon, a =CH2 with no H on the neighboring carbon. That is CH2=C(CH3)CO2CH3, methyl methacrylate. The C=O at 1720 rather than about 1740 fits conjugation with the C=C.
x: Methyl (E)-but-2-enoate has two vinyl H on adjacent carbons; they split each other (large trans J) and are split by the CH3, so they are not singlets, and its CH3 would be a doublet of doublets, not a singlet.
Ethyl acrylate would show an OCH<sub>2</sub> quartet and a CH<sub>3</sub> triplet, and three vinyl H that split each other.
Allyl acetate has a CH<sub>3</sub>C=O singlet near 2.1 but an OCH<sub>2</sub> doublet near 4.6 and three coupled vinyl H; its non-conjugated ester C=O would be near 1740.

q: A compound containing only C, H and N shows M<sup>+</sup> at m/z 69. Its IR spectrum has a sharp, medium band at 2250 cm<sup>−1</sup> and nothing above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>. Its <sup>13</sup>C NMR spectrum shows four signals: δ 119.8, 19.3, 19.1 and 13.4. Which structure fits?
h: An odd molecular mass means an odd number of N atoms. Then use the IR band and the number of <sup>13</sup>C signals.
w: By the nitrogen rule, an odd M+ (69) means an odd number of nitrogens, so C4H7N with one N. The 2250 cm−1 band is a C≡N stretch, and there is no N–H or ≡C–H band above 3000. The 13C peak at 119.8 is the nitrile carbon, and three more signals below 20 ppm mean three different sp3 carbons. Butanenitrile, CH3CH2CH2C≡N, fits.
x: 2-Methylpropanenitrile is also C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>7</sub>N with a C≡N, but its two CH<sub>3</sub> groups are equivalent, so it gives only three <sup>13</sup>C signals.
But-3-yn-1-amine has N–H stretches and a strong ≡C–H band near 3300, and its alkyne carbons appear near 70–85 ppm, not 120.
2-Butyn-1-amine has N–H bands above 3000 cm<sup>−1</sup>, and its internal alkyne carbons appear near 75–80 ppm; there is no 120 ppm nitrile carbon.

q: Which compound gives a <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum of exactly two singlets with integrals in a 3 : 1 ratio?
h: Count the H in each set and reduce the ratio.
w: tert-Butyl methyl ether has nine equivalent H on the tert-butyl group and three on the OCH3. Neither group has H on a neighboring carbon, so both signals are singlets, in a 9 : 3 = 3 : 1 ratio. tert-Butyl methyl ether.
x: Methyl acetate gives two 3H singlets, a 1 : 1 ratio.
2,2-Dimethoxypropane gives two 6H singlets, a 1 : 1 ratio.
1-Chloro-2,2-dimethylpropane gives a 9H singlet and a 2H singlet, a 4.5 : 1 ratio.

q: A chlorotoluene shows two doublets of 2H each in the aromatic region of its <sup>1</sup>H NMR spectrum, plus a 3H singlet near 2.3 ppm. Which isomer is it?
h: Which substitution pattern makes the four ring H into two equivalent pairs?
w: In a para-disubstituted ring with two different groups, a mirror plane makes the four ring H into two pairs. Each H is split by its one ortho neighbor, giving two 2H doublets. 4-Chlorotoluene (para) fits.
x: 2-Chlorotoluene (ortho) has four different ring H, giving a more complex pattern of 1H signals.
3-Chlorotoluene (meta) also has four different ring H, including an isolated H between the two groups.
Benzyl chloride is C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub>Cl too, but it has five ring H and a CH<sub>2</sub>Cl singlet near 4.6, not a CH<sub>3</sub> at 2.3.

q: How many signals appear in the broadband-decoupled 13C NMR spectrum of 4-tert-butylcyclohexanone (shown)?
h: A mirror plane runs through C1, C4 and the tert-butyl group. Count carbons on one side of it.
w: The mirror plane through C=O (C1), C4 and the tert-butyl group makes C2 and C6 equivalent and C3 and C5 equivalent. Signals: C=O, C2/C6, C3/C5, C4, the quaternary C of tert-butyl, and the three equivalent CH3. Total 6.
x: Five misses one environment, usually by merging the quaternary tert-butyl carbon with the CH3 groups or with C4.
Seven treats the three tert-butyl methyls as two kinds; they are equivalent.
Ten counts every carbon separately and ignores the symmetry.
